claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of an fcc matrix and hexagonal C14 Laves precipitates.
The FeCoNiTi system exhibits ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Rapid quenching stabilizes the dual fcc+C14 microstructure in FeCoNiTi.
The C14 Laves phase in FeCoNiTi contains a Ti-rich sublattice.
The Ti sublattice of the C14 phase carries a magnetic moment.
Ti moments in the C14 phase couple antiferromagnetically to Fe, Co, and Ni moments in the fcc matrix across the fcc/C14 interface.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling partially cancels Fe/Co/Ni moments and lowers the net saturation magnetization attributed to the fcc phase.
Magnetic-anisotropy mismatch and structural discontinuity at fcc/C14 boundaries create domain-wall pinning energy wells.
The pinned domain-wall network and enhanced magnetic anisotropy raise the coercivity of dual-phase FeCoNiTi.
The proposed interfacial mechanism produces a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase alloy has lower saturation magnetization than a single-phase fcc reference.
Interfacial coupling shifts the magnetic transition temperatures of the dual-phase alloy.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and the absence of secondary-phase pinning.
Increasing and optimizing fcc/C14 interface density will maximize magnetic coupling effects.
Coherent or semi-coherent fcc/C14 interfaces are required to sustain the proposed exchange coupling.
The proposed mechanism fails if the C14 phase is nonmagnetic or the fcc/C14 interface is fully incoherent.
Phase decomposition in AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi decreases saturation magnetization and increases coercivity relative to the single-phase state.
Secondary Laves phases are intrinsically brittle and can limit ambient-temperature tensile ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys.
